findings.where: Screen 2 (All of it as work), pressure–volume chart
findings.what: The chart draws a flat, steady-pressure push-out, but at steady pressure a growing volume means a hotter ideal gas (lesson 3's pV ÷ T rule), so its internal energy must rise, not stay at the 0 J answer; draw a falling curve (pressure dropping as it expands) instead of a flat line.

The chart draws a flat, steady-pressure squeeze, but an ideal gas squeezed at steady pressure gets cooler and loses internal energy, which contradicts the 'up 200 J' answer; draw a rising curve (pressure climbing as it is squeezed), as screen 3's push already does.

"No engine can beat the Carnot limit" states the contested point as settled, then two sentences later the screen says how far it binds a real diesel is debated; qualify it as the explain does: "No engine working between a hot side and a cold side can beat...".

findings.where: Screen 1 text and cylinder label, and explain paragraph 2
findings.what: "200 kPa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J" multiplies to 0.2 when checked by hand, because the kPa-to-Pa step is skipped; write 200,000 Pa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J, which also shows that pascals times cubic metres are newton-metres, or joules.

findings.where: Screens 7, 9 and 11, the shaded 'typical: 60 to 70%' block

findings.where: Screen 7, live split labels (moved state, 360 px)
findings.what: The work flow's label has no kW under it, while cooling and exhaust each show one; it is also pushed off-centre with a leader line because hidden generator words ('electrical output', 'cooler must carry') take up width on screens without a generator; show the work's kW and measure only the words that are showing.

The reason the cooling is needed is in the explain but not on the screen: squeezed while still hot, the gas would push back as hard and take back all the work. Without it, "No loop can skip it" arrives unexplained; swap it in for "The cooling is the heat given out." to stay under 90 words.

The labels put heat in only on the left side and heat out only on the right, but on this rectangular loop the gas also takes in heat while pushing out hot and gives heat out while squeezed cool; mark the heat-in label along the top and the heat-out label along the bottom too, or say 'mostly'.
"People call that heat a loss" has no heat to point back to, because the sentence before is "That is the first law."; name it: "People call the cooling and exhaust heat a loss".
"Or the gas keeps the energy inside itself" reads as either-or, but the example then does both; try "What it does not spend as work, it keeps inside as internal energy."
"A maker claims 75% from an engine" does not say 75% of what; say "claims 75% of its fuel energy as work".
"400 kW of electrical output from 40% of its fuel" can read as burning only 40% of its fuel; say "its output is 40% of its fuel energy".

The 7.1 kg/s distractor needs fresh water's 4,200 J, which the screen never shows while the question states 3,850 J, so it tests nothing; a real slip such as leaving out the 10 °C (about 78 kg/s) would teach more.

The brief promised the diesel in outline: compression ignition, only air compressed so a higher compression ratio, and four or two strokes. None of it appears; one or two sentences in the diesel paragraph would keep the promise.
